comments.author: @MediaCreators
comments.text: I completely agree with you! I have a strong sense that some of these "autonomous" demonstrations are reminiscent of the THERANOS and NIKOLA situations. I have previous experience working with SARCOS in the 90s, where their robot "LOU" could be controlled by a sensor suit and was already capable of performing essentially everything we witness today. I'm not implying that this is the case with FIGURE, but it's prudent to exercise caution. Given the substantial investments of hundreds of billions of dollars from various investors, the temptation for such actions might be present.

I had the same impression as you, @WesRoth
I watched a video where a human does 95% of the work for a robot.
I wonder, if the robot needs a human present to place the mug in the machine, what is the purpose of this robot?
Do I need to get up from the table, go to where the coffee machine is, place the coffee pod on the table, then put my mug in the machine and tell the robot, 'Make coffee'?

They seemed very 'lost' in what they were doing to me, but the end of the interview was dramatic when they were asked to call the robot, and you clearly hear nervousness in the voice and laughter afterward, along with an excuse to change the subject.

comments.author: @PierreH1968
comments.text: It is interesting that researchers are trying to modify the environment to fit the Robot's reach or capabilities (like changing the coffee maker type so it is easier to access for the robot) instead of working on mapping robots to the human environment... We need to shape robots as closely as possible to humans. From ergonomics to anthropomorphic familiarity and societal integration it is best to shape robots for us than to shape the environment to them. Once we solve this challenge, all challenges will be easy to solve.
